newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan central bank cautions forex speculators.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan central bank cautions forex speculators.

text.p: Central bank vice governor Liang Cheng-chin, in a clear caution to foreign exchange speculators, said a southeast Asia-style currency crisis could "never happen here" because Taiwan can marshal "appropriate" defences.

"Our situation is entirely different from southeast Asian countries," Liang told reporters after the close of trading. "The currency crisis that happened in Thailand, the Philippines, Indonesia and Malaysia could never happen here."

Liang was asked about whether the central bank would defend the Taiwan dollar if it came under attack by speculators, as occurred in southeast Asia in recent weeks, seriously undermining the value of several regional currencies.
"We hope the foreign exchange market participants can fully understand our situation," he replied, using language that analysts interpreted as a clear caution.
"If the participants do not understand the situation, the central bank will deal with this with appropriate measures."
Liang declined to say what those measures might be or describe the specific circumstances under which they would be ordered.
Taiwan's currency has come under occasional speculative pressure in July, local and offshore interests apparently testing the central bank's bottom line.

Analysts and dealers say that in each instance, the central bank -- armed with more than US$90 billion in reserves -- has responded with quiet but firm intervention, often in the final minutes of trade to stave off significant declines.

The Taiwan dollar, which closed on Wednesday at T$27.939 to the U.S. dollar, slipped as low as T$27.967 on Thursday -- only to recover to Wednesday's closing level in the final minutes on what dealers called active central bank intervention.

Turnover through dealers on Thursday was extremely heavy at US$349.50 million -- US$83 million of which came in the final 15 minutes of trading, when official intervention was the most pronounced, dealers said.
"The central bank did not want to see speculators earn a profit, so it purposely brought the Taiwan dollar to an even close," said one dealer at a foreign bank.

Dealers said the central bank likely would allow the Taiwan dollar to continue on what has been a gradual depreciation dating to the beginning of 1997, with the aim of stimulating exports, but it would not tolerate volatile movements.
